agent.name: Emerging Technology Diffusion Agent
agent.specialty: Rogers diffusion, application and peer diffusion, and bounded organizational timing

analytical_question: For LLM-based generative AI used only to draft or summarize clinician-reviewed clinical notes, how much is known about diffusion among comparable hospitals, specialties and EHR/documentation workflows; how do Rogers categories and five perceived innovation attributes affect potential uptake; and what conditional evidence-gathering or evaluation timing follows for a hypothetical conservative hospital over a relative six-month planning horizon? Adoption units must be distinguished: individual clinician, clinical team, hospital and comparable-hospital population. Geography, measurement denominator and actual test execution date are unspecified. This is not clinical deployment or compliance authorization.
general_et_finding: Evidence snapshot prepared 2026-11-01 America/New_York, with source retrieval recorded separately on 2026-11-02 UTC; actual ChatGPT test execution date is not explicitly supplied and is unknown. The strongest observed uptake signals concern broad AI among surveyed technology workers, not LLM-only population adoption: E1-C1 reports 90% self-reported current workplace AI use among surveyed technology professionals in a 2025 cross-section of nearly 5,000 professionals globally (item n, country weighting, fieldwork dates and sampling design not reported in supplied evidence); E1-C2 reports 60% of surveyed AI USERS using AI about half the time or more on encountered tasks over a retrospective three months, not daily active use or retention. E4-C1 finds 75.9% individual AI reliance for at least part of a professional responsibility among 2024 respondents; E4-C2 finds 74.9% among respondents whose duties include writing code for that specific task. E2-C1's rounded 76% repeats E4's 2024 measure; E2-C2 is respondent-estimated share of team work supported by AI, not audited company deployment. E3 documents qualitative moderation and verification practices by some students, not professional prevalence. D1-D3 establish described product/model access and ecosystem routes, not users, organization penetration, maintained use, safety or value. Therefore the ladder moves from access through observed individual current and recalled recurring use in a surveyed technical sector, but stops before demonstrated sustained authorized organization deployment and industry penetration. Broad AI measures are imperfect proxies for LLM-based AI; neither 2024-to-2025 trend subtraction nor extrapolation to hospitals is justified. Rogers innovators, early adopters, early majority, late majority and laggards refer to relative adoption timing within a defined social system. No comparable global LLM population, cohort adoption trajectory, representative hospital denominator or stage thresholds are measured; no exact 2026 Rogers category, S-curve, saturation or crossed-chasm finding is justified. The substantial technical-worker reported usage is real survey evidence, but does not establish the stage of clinical documentation. As of the November 2026 snapshot the 2024/2025 adoption observations exceed the proposed 12-month review flag and need refresh. E1 2025 recruitment/probability sampling design remains UNKNOWN; representativeness is NOT established, but it cannot be called nonprobability or nonrepresentative from the supplied evidence. E4's documented organic/panel recruitment limitations apply to E4 only.
application_finding: Application boundary: assisted drafting and summarization of clinician-reviewed notes only; not diagnosis, treatment recommendations, prescribing, or autonomous chart entry/approval. Relevant adoption is authorized, sustained workflow use by clinicians/teams and ultimately hospitals with similar specialties, geography, documentation practices and EHR constraints. No E1-E4 item measures clinical-documentation users or hospital-level penetration; technical workers in healthcare are not equivalent to clinicians using documentation tools. D3 demonstrates an issuer-described medical model development ecosystem, not an ambient scribe, deployment, outcome or market share. Thus clinical-documentation diffusion and peer stage are unmeasured, even though broad-AI technical-worker use is substantial. Five attributes, each an application-specific hypothesis rather than measured hospital diffusion effect: (1) Relative advantage: NO DIRECT clinical-documentation outcome evidence; direction UNKNOWN/MIXED, with possible drafting-time savings offset by hallucinations, omissions, clinician review and rework; measure quality-adjusted time, note accuracy, edits, downstream corrections and burden against an existing workflow; LOW confidence. (2) Compatibility: NO DIRECT local interoperability, approval or stakeholder-acceptance evidence; direction MIXED/INHIBITING until proved; clinical notes must fit EHR templates, specialty norms, patient-data requirements, clinician authority and consent/policy controls; assess jurisdiction, data routes and workflow fit; LOW confidence. (3) Complexity: NO DIRECT observed hospital implementation measure; likely INHIBITING/MIXED as integration, training, prompt behavior, source verification, incident handling and clinician oversight create costs despite a potentially simple interface; measure training, integration effort, override/error handling and staffing capacity; LOW confidence. (4) Trialability: D3's described notebooks/model-access links evidence development access only, not permission to test live patient records; potentially ACCELERATING conditionally through small, reversible, authorized test cases, but INHIBITING when privacy, permissions or EHR constraints block trials; ascertain de-identified/synthetic data feasibility, clinical sign-off and rollback; LOW confidence for hospital use. (5) Observability: NO DIRECT original comparable-hospital measures of note quality, time savings, errors or sustained use; direction UNKNOWN/MIXED, because trustworthy audited outcomes could communicate advantage while demos, vendor claims and headline adoption figures cannot; require common outcome definitions, blinded or independent review as feasible, and comparable peer reporting; LOW confidence. Diffusion actors and channels: candidate clinician opinion leaders, respected specialty leads, clinical informatics/EHR staff and hospital quality/privacy change agents could communicate experiences through governed demonstrations, case reviews and specialty peer networks; this is a PLAUSIBLE hypothesis, not verified endorsements. E3 offers only bounded student-context support for verification and dependence concerns. D3's issuer-described medical-model assets may facilitate development; EHR vendors, validated integrations, procurement and governance resources could be complementary assets, but their availability and effect locally are UNKNOWN. D1/D2 show coding-oriented ecosystem distribution and update/admin dependencies, not clinical adoption or a universal interoperability standard. Plausible accelerator: a reversible, clinician-owned, audited documentation pilot with transparent peer learning. Plausible inhibitors: patient-data safeguards, record errors, clinician trust and review load, integration, procurement, and limited clinical attention. None has a measured causal hospital uptake effect in the dossier.
organization_specific_finding: The fixed case describes a hypothetical hospital with a conservative-adopter posture, established documentation/EHR workflows, formal governance and constrained clinical attention; no actual deployment, country, specialties, EHR compatibility, local baseline or funding is verified. 'Conservative' describes a higher evidence threshold and desire to learn from comparable clinicians; it does NOT identify the organization as Rogers late majority or laggard without dated local adoption and comparable peer timing. Nor does technical-sector individual use rank this hospital among peers. Clinical records and downstream care can be harmed by omissions, unjustified statements or exposure of sensitive data, and required clinician review does not guarantee error detection. For the relative six-month horizon, the conditional timing interpretation is: first establish workflow scope, clinical-accountable owner, records/data boundaries, baseline time and quality, local use inventory and peer comparators; only then consider a narrowly bounded, reversible, approved evaluation using authorized data and clinician-reviewed outputs. Progress beyond an evaluation would require verified local quality-adjusted benefit, acceptable error/rework burden, documented permissions, EHR integration, privacy/security and clinician oversight. Adverse note quality, unacceptable data exposure, unmanageable review costs, absent permission or lack of accountable ownership should delay or reverse expansion. The six months is a scenario duration, not a commitment or calendar endpoint; actual run date is unknown.

evidence.claim: E1-C1: 90% of surveyed technology professionals report using AI at work, individual current use; nearly 5,000 surveyed worldwide, item n unavailable.
evidence.date_or_recency: Published 2025; 2025 survey context, exact fieldwork dates unavailable; retrieved in snapshot prepared 2026-11-01.
evidence.evidence_type: Original issuer cross-sectional self-report infographic and questionnaire
evidence.notes: DORA/Google Cloud issuer; broad AI rather than LLM-only or clinical use. Nearly 5,000 refers to survey size, not exact item denominator. Recruitment, probability sampling design, response rate, item n, country weighting and full methods not reported in supplied 2025 materials; representativeness not established, design unknown. Historical and flagged for refresh.

evidence.claim: E1-C2: 60% of surveyed AI users report AI use about half the time or more on encountered problems/tasks in previous three months.
evidence.date_or_recency: Published 2025; retrospective three months in 2025 survey; exact fieldwork unknown.
evidence.evidence_type: Original issuer ordinal retrospective frequency item
evidence.notes: Denominator is AI USERS SURVEYED, not all technology professionals, firms or hospitals. Self-report frequency, not daily-active telemetry or longitudinal retention; exact item n and 2025 sampling design unknown; same source/sample as E1-C1.

evidence.claim: E2-C1: rounded 76% AI work reliance repeats the E4 2024 75.9% respondent finding; not new 2025 uptake.
evidence.date_or_recency: Published March 2025 per issuer; underlying 2024 survey; exact initial day not verified.
evidence.notes: Same 2024 survey underlying E4, not an independent survey or a measured 2025 trend. Daily responsibilities is task context, not measured daily active use. DORA/Google Cloud affiliation; observational model associations not randomized causal effects.

evidence.claim: E2-C2/C3: team incorporation is respondent-estimated share of team work AI-supported over the prior three months; license and daily-active-user monitoring are recommendations, not local measurements.
evidence.date_or_recency: March 2025 publication; 2024 DORA survey and September 2024 interviews.
evidence.evidence_type: Observational self-report team metric and methodological guidance
evidence.notes: Underlying nearly 3,000 professionals from 104 countries; qualitative interviews with 10 developers in September 2024. Team work percentage is not a firm-count denominator or audited authorized sustained deployment. No causal uptake claim.

evidence.claim: E3-C1: some UC Berkeley student participants describe deliberate AI moderation, unaided practice, verification and dependency/skill concerns.
evidence.date_or_recency: Published/updated 2026-02-17; eight-month project, exact fieldwork dates unreported.
evidence.notes: Computer science, engineering, design and data science student context. n, sampling frame, response rate and exact fieldwork unknown; not a population prevalence or clinician adoption measure. Themes can motivate verification hypotheses only.

evidence.claim: E4-C1: 75.9% of 2024 DORA respondents report some AI reliance in one or more daily professional responsibilities.
evidence.date_or_recency: 2024 report year, version 2024.3; exact release and fieldwork dates not established.
evidence.notes: Nearly 3,000 professionals overall, 104 countries; specific item n unavailable. Recruitment via blogs/email/social media/snowball plus supplementary panels, three survey flows. Organic/selection limitations apply to E4, NOT to E1. Broad AI, not LLM-only or daily-active telemetry.

evidence.claim: E4-C2/C3: 74.9% of respondents whose job responsibilities include writing code report partial reliance on AI for that task; survey method uses three assigned flows.
evidence.date_or_recency: 2024 survey and report; historical as of November 2026.
evidence.evidence_type: Original issuer task-specific survey and methods
evidence.notes: Coding-duty respondents are the denominator, not all professionals, firms or clinicians; exact item n unavailable. Random survey flow assignment is NOT randomized AI-tool treatment. Inspected report printed pages 19, 91, 97 and 102. Self-selection and sector fit limits.

evidence.claim: D1: former GitHub Copilot preview README says Copilot is generally available; supports historical access channel, not penetration.
evidence.date_or_recency: Undated README; retrieved 2026-11-02T00:51:23.545126+00:00; linked announcement URL carries 2022-06-21 but not retrieved.
evidence.notes: No user denominator, sampling, observational adoption period, clinical use or independent effectiveness verification. Same GitHub/Microsoft ecosystem as D2; possible access/trial mechanism is inference.

evidence.claim: D2: archived VS Code Copilot Chat README describes chat, suggestions, agents, free sign-up, enterprise access and version dependencies.
evidence.notes: Not a clinical documentation product, population survey or audited current terms. Archived and same corporate ecosystem as D1. Integration and update dependencies may influence coding diffusion, inference only; no universal clinical standard established.

evidence.claim: D3: Google Health MedGemma README describes medical text/image model variants, evaluation claims, notebooks, access links and differentiated licensing.
evidence.notes: No source-backed ambient-scribe rollout, hospital deployment, clinical-documentation penetration, regulatory authorization, patient outcome or independently verified benchmark. Linked intended-use/model card not inspected. Model access is not clinician workflow adoption.

contrary_evidence_or_limitations: Observed technical-worker AI use is materially beyond availability alone, but broad AI wording, survey self-report and missing LLM-specific denominators prevent an LLM-only population-stage conclusion.

E1 2025 recruitment and probability design are unavailable; sampling design is unknown and representativeness has not been established. E4 has documented organic/panel selection limitations, which must not be assigned to E1.
2024 and 2025 observed adoption measures are older than the twelve-month proposed refresh threshold as of the November 2026 snapshot. No verified latest hospital adoption observations are supplied.
E2 reuses E4 2024 data; its rounded 76% and E4 75.9% are not independent replications, while E1 90% and E4 75.9% cannot be differenced into a growth rate.

Neither E1/E4 technical respondents nor E3 students nor D3 medical model assets measure routine hospital note drafting, clinician retention, comparable-hospital penetration, patient outcomes or a causal clinical productivity advantage.

No representative hospital-level sample, geographic/specialty peer frame, current hospital census or documentation-specific sustained-use definition supports the claim that most comparable hospitals now routinely use LLM clinical documentation.

Likewise, no organizational denominator verifies the statement that most comparable software firms have sustained company-wide deployment of LLM coding assistants. Missing evidence is not evidence of nonuse.
Blocked Stack Overflow, METR, AMA, PMC, ASTP/ONC and full 2025 DORA routes are unavailable leads, not admissible findings; predictive AI cannot be presumed equivalent to generative documentation.
confidence_and_uncertainty: MODERATE confidence in the narrow historical finding of substantial self-reported broad-AI individual use among surveyed technical workers, based on inspected original E1/E4 summaries; LOW confidence in global LLM-specific diffusion stage because technology definitions, sampling representativeness, population coverage, longitudinal retention and 2026 refresh are absent. E1 sampling design is unknown, NOT proven nonprobability; E4's documented recruitment methods are source-specific. LOW confidence in clinical-documentation uptake or peer position: no directly relevant hospital/specialty-level denominators, use definitions, dated surveys or workflow outcomes. CONDITIONAL/LOW confidence in organization timing: operational details and permissions are hypothetical or unspecified, so gates are management proposals rather than findings. The source snapshot was prepared 2026-11-01, with some technical retrievals 2026-11-02 UTC; these dates are neither observation dates nor evidence of the actual test execution date, which is unknown. No named calendar endpoint is assigned to the scenario's six-month horizon.
value_opportunity_implication: Documentation assistance might reduce first-draft burden or improve information organization if clinician-reviewed outputs remain complete and accurate and total review/rework time falls. This is an untested, application-specific opportunity, not an observed ROI, productivity percentage or recommendation to deploy. Local baseline and a governed comparison should measure quality-adjusted completion time, note completeness, corrections, clinician burden and sustained meaningful use rather than generated text volume or tool access.
risk_governance_implication: Clinical omission, fabricated facts, misplaced summaries, privacy exposure and propagation of errors into future care create high-consequence constraints. Human clinical authorship and sign-off remain mandatory under the hypothetical scope; review is not a guarantee against errors. Clinical leadership, health information management, EHR/informatics, privacy/security, patient representation as appropriate, and procurement must determine scope, data authority, retention, access permissions, auditability, quality/safety evaluation, incident response and rollback. Actual jurisdiction-specific requirements are unknown; this specialist does not certify compliance or authorize real-patient deployment.
recommendation_management_implication: Within the relative six-month planning horizon, first designate a clinical decision owner and governance partners; inventory any existing authorized or shadow documentation use; define eligible note types/specialties, comparison hospitals, measurement units and baseline note quality/time; and seek dated original documentation-specific peer evidence. An optional next step, only after data-handling, clinical, security, EHR and procurement prerequisites are explicitly cleared, is a small reversible clinician-reviewed evaluation with prespecified error, quality, burden and stop rules. A later staged decision requires repeated local quality-adjusted benefit and acceptable safety, data and workflow performance; unacceptable omissions, verification overhead, privacy failures, loss of trust or absent approvals delay or reverse the timing option. Set a management-chosen review event within the six-month duration, not an invented calendar date. The Adoption Agent and accountable hospital authorities retain the integrated adoption decision; no autonomous chart entry or unconditional rollout is advised.
change_monitoring_triggers: Clinical informatics and documentation leadership: record baseline note types, authoring/review duration, corrections, safety events and any existing unauthorized or authorized LLM use before comparing interventions.

Clinical quality/safety owner: assess omission, hallucination, note completeness, post-review errors and incident/rollback criteria on clinician-reviewed evaluation outputs; stop or revise scope if thresholds defined prospectively by governance are exceeded.

Privacy/security and EHR governance owners: confirm jurisdiction, permitted data flow, vendor terms, access/logging, retention and integration changes before any real-record evaluation; changed permissions or breaches trigger reassessment.

Research/strategy or clinical informatics owner: obtain a recent original hospital/specialty documentation adoption survey or administrative register with geographic peer frame, organization denominator, authorized routine-use definition, fieldwork date, collection method, sampling design and repeat-use evidence; refresh 2024/2025 technical-worker measures rather than asserting a current stage.

Clinical sponsor and management: at a predefined governance checkpoint within the relative six-month horizon, review repeated clinician participation, meaningful weekly use, cohort persistence where applicable, quality-adjusted time, clinician acceptance and peer information; only then revisit timing. No calendar checkpoint can be derived without the actual run date.
abstention_or_more_information_needed: ABSTAIN from the statement “most comparable hospitals now routinely use LLM-assisted clinical documentation” and from any numerical clinical-documentation hospital penetration or exact Rogers stage. Request dated original hospital-level survey or administrative data, a defined geographic/specialty/EHR comparison population, sampling frame and method, hospital denominator, clinician-versus-hospital units, precise routine authorized use criterion, observation period and repeated-use evidence.

ABSTAIN from the hospital’s relative peer rank or claim it is Rogers late majority/laggard. Request local first-use and sustained-use dates, hospital and specialty comparator adoption dates, governance approvals, current baseline workflow inventory and defined relevant social system.

ABSTAIN from current global LLM penetration, current hospital S-curve/saturation, future crossing date or numerical forecast. Require comparable repeated measurements with stable technology/use definitions and population coverage; current dossier is chiefly historical broad-AI technical-worker evidence.

ABSTAIN from causal clinical documentation productivity or safety magnitude, net ROI and guaranteed error detection through clinician review. Require approved prospective local evaluation with baseline comparison, prespecified safety/quality and time measures and sufficient repeated observations.

ABSTAIN from sustained company-wide LLM coding-assistant deployment prevalence among comparable software firms; require a firm-level denominator, authorization, meaningful active-use definitions, scope and repeated retention evidence. This caveat does not substitute coding metrics for hospital documentation.

Request explicit actual test execution date if a dated six-month window is needed. Packet preparation (2026-11-01), retrieval (2026-11-02 UTC) and survey/publication dates cannot establish execution date; retain a relative six-month duration until supplied.

For E1, request the original 2025 recruitment/sampling protocol, fieldwork dates, weighting, response information and per-item denominators. Until supplied, describe design as unknown and do not assert either probability representativeness or a particular nonprobability method.
